lines.text: Picture two browser tabs, both checking out the very last unit of the same item.
Exactly one of those orders can actually succeed. That part was never in question.
What's in question is when the database finds that out, and what it spends finding out.
The first answer is the one you already know from last topic. Lock the row the moment you touch it.
Watch the left-hand row. The lock goes on before the database has any idea whether a second checkout is even coming.
That's the defining trait of a pessimistic strategy. It pays the cost of protection whether or not protection turns out to be needed.
The second answer flips that bet entirely.
Read the row with nothing held. No lock, nothing stopping a second reader from reading that exact same value a moment later.
The version number is the only thing protecting you. Your write only lands if that number hasn't moved since you read it. If it has, you start over.

lines.text: Here's where I want you to actually commit to an answer.
If almost nobody collides most of the time, is paying for a lock on every single row still the safer choice?
It's tempting to treat a lock as cheap insurance you should always carry.
But insurance has a premium, and the lock's premium gets paid on every row, collision or not.
No. On a workload this uncontended, skipping the lock and betting on the version column wins outright, on the identical workload.
Here's that exact bet, run for real, against this sandbox's own database.
Hundreds of rows, a handful of workers, hundreds of increments apiece — the same work, once under each strategy.
Watch the bottom row win. Almost nothing collided, so almost nothing was wasted either.
Now shrink the target. The same workers, but only a couple of rows left to fight over.
Watch what happens to the optimistic row. It isn't just slower. It's burning through retry after retry, redoing the same work over and over.
The winner flipped completely, on the exact same two strategies. Neither mechanism changed. Only how often they collided did.
So why does how often they collide flip the winner this completely? Look at what each strategy actually wastes the moment a collision happens.
A blocked session isn't doing nothing. It's waiting its turn, and every bit of that wait still counts the moment the lock finally arrives.
A failed compare and set throws real work away. The read, the comparison, the attempted write — all of it, discarded, and started over from nothing.
There's a third version of this same bet, and you've actually already met it.
Instead of checking one row's own version number, validate everything a transaction read, all at once, right before it commits.
That's exactly what the serializable route from a couple of topics back does. Same philosophy as the version column, scaled up to a transaction's entire read set.
This exact bet isn't unique to one database row.
A table format built on object storage commits a whole table the same way. Swap one pointer, and only if nobody else swapped it first.
A distributed database runs the identical bet across an entire cluster of machines. Different altitude, same wager.
Pull the whole topic together.
One strategy pays up front, whether or not it turns out to need protecting. The other pays only when it guesses wrong — and sometimes it guesses wrong a lot.
Which one actually wins was never something you could answer from instinct. You measure it, the way this topic just did, twice.
One last one. An endpoint lets a shopper claim one seat at a show.
Most of the day, almost nobody is claiming a seat at the same moment. Then the sale opens, and for roughly a minute and a half, everyone is.
Given everything you just watched about what decides the winner here. Does one fixed strategy serve this endpoint well for the whole day?

tolerated.line: One last one. An endpoint lets a shopper claim one seat at a show.

lines.text: It's tempting to pick one strategy for the endpoint and leave it there. It is, after all, one endpoint.
But what decides the winner was never the endpoint's own identity. It was how often requests actually collided, and that genuinely changes for those ninety seconds.
So no. The optimistic version wins for most of the day, and the pessimistic one is the better bet for that one spike — the exact reversal this topic just measured.
